title: Circuits I
description: Circuits I develops DC and AC circuit analysis from elements and Kirchhoff's laws through resistive networks, equivalents, op-amps, RC/RL/RLC transients, phasors, power, filters, and practical measurement and simulation.

topics.title: Circuit Elements and Electrical Quantities
topics.description: This opening section gives students the vocabulary of circuits: what voltage, current, resistance, capacitance, inductance, and power mean physically and mathematically.

children.title: Voltage, current, charge, and power
children.description: These quantities are the language used to describe what a circuit is doing and whether energy is being stored, delivered, or dissipated.

children.title: Reference directions and passive sign convention
Resistors
children.description: Resistors provide the simplest model of electrical opposition and are the building blocks for dividers, loads, and bias networks.

children.title: Capacitors
children.description: Capacitors store energy in electric fields, making them central to timing, filtering, coupling, and transient behavior.

children.title: Inductors
children.description: Inductors store energy in magnetic fields and shape current dynamics, filters, power conversion, and electromagnetic behavior.

topics.title: Ohm's Law and Kirchhoff's Laws
topics.description: Circuit analysis rests on local component laws plus network conservation laws. This section turns circuit diagrams into solvable equations.

children.title: Ohm's law
children.description: Ohm's law connects voltage, current, and resistance in linear resistive elements.

children.title: Kirchhoff's current law
children.description: KCL expresses charge conservation at circuit nodes and is the foundation of nodal analysis.

children.title: Current entering and leaving a node
Kirchhoff's voltage law
children.description: KVL expresses energy conservation around loops and is the foundation of mesh analysis.

children.title: Dependent and independent sources in loops
Source models
children.description: Sources represent the external energy or signal inputs that drive a circuit.

topics.title: Resistive Circuit Analysis
topics.description: Before adding dynamics and AC behavior, students need fluency with resistive networks, equivalent resistance, and source/load interactions.

children.title: Series and parallel reduction
children.description: Reduction methods simplify networks while preserving the behavior seen at chosen terminals.

children.title: Voltage and current division
children.description: Divider rules are fast analysis tools and practical design patterns.

children.title: Dependent-source circuits
children.description: Dependent sources model amplifiers and controlled behavior, so they prepare students for op-amps and electronics.

children.title: Linearity and superposition
children.description: Superposition lets students separate source contributions in linear circuits.

topics.title: Nodal and Mesh Analysis
topics.description: Nodal and mesh methods are systematic equation-building techniques. They replace guesswork with repeatable procedures for circuits that cannot be simplified by inspection.

children.title: Nodal analysis
children.description: Nodal analysis solves for node voltages using KCL and is usually the most general method for circuit work.

children.title: Supernodes
children.description: Supernodes handle voltage sources between non-reference nodes without breaking KCL logic.

children.title: Mesh analysis
children.description: Mesh analysis solves for loop currents using KVL and is efficient for planar circuits.

children.title: Supermeshes and method selection
children.description: Supermeshes handle current sources between meshes, while method selection teaches students to choose the least painful analysis route.

topics.title: Thevenin and Norton Equivalents
topics.description: Equivalent circuits compress a complicated network into a simpler source-resistance model, which is invaluable for loading, power transfer, and modular design.

children.title: Terminal behavior
children.description: Equivalent circuits preserve what an external load sees at a pair of terminals.

children.title: Thevenin equivalent
children.description: Thevenin form turns a linear network into one voltage source and one resistance.

children.title: Norton equivalent
children.description: Norton form uses a current source and parallel resistance, giving an alternate but equivalent view.

children.title: Maximum power transfer
children.description: Power-transfer analysis shows how load choice changes delivered power and efficiency.

topics.title: Operational Amplifiers
topics.description: Op-amps bridge circuit analysis and practical electronics by using feedback to create predictable amplifiers, buffers, summing circuits, and active filters.

children.title: Ideal op-amp assumptions
children.description: The ideal model lets students analyze feedback circuits without immediately wrestling with device physics.

children.title: Negative feedback configurations
children.description: Feedback topologies create stable, useful relationships between input and output.

children.title: Signal-conditioning circuits
children.description: Op-amps are practical tools for scaling, combining, and shaping signals.

children.title: Nonideal behavior
children.description: Nonideal limits explain why real circuits depart from ideal calculations.

topics.title: First-Order Circuits: RC and RL Transients
topics.description: First-order circuits introduce time dependence. Students learn how stored energy changes after switching events and how time constants shape response speed.

children.title: Switching behavior
children.description: Switches create initial-value problems that reveal how capacitors and inductors respond over time.

children.title: RC circuits
children.description: RC circuits are the foundation of timing, smoothing, coupling, and simple filtering.

children.title: RL circuits
children.description: RL circuits describe current buildup and decay in inductive systems.

children.title: General first-order solution
children.description: A unified solution form helps students recognize the same mathematics across RC and RL cases.

topics.title: Second-Order Circuits: RLC Dynamics
topics.description: RLC circuits introduce oscillation, damping, resonance, and richer transient behavior that later connect to filters and frequency response.

children.title: Series and parallel RLC models
children.description: RLC models combine energy storage in electric and magnetic fields with resistive dissipation.

children.title: Natural response
children.description: The natural response shows what a circuit does after stored energy is released without a continuing input.

children.title: Step response
children.description: Step response connects source changes to underdamped, critically damped, or overdamped circuit behavior.

children.title: Resonance
children.description: Resonance explains why circuits can selectively amplify or suppress signals near particular frequencies.

topics.title: AC Steady-State Analysis
topics.description: AC steady-state analysis lets students analyze sinusoidal circuits without solving differential equations every time.

children.title: Sinusoidal signals
children.description: Sinusoids are the standard model for power systems, signals, oscillators, and frequency-domain testing.

children.title: Complex representation
children.description: Complex numbers encode magnitude and phase compactly for sinusoidal analysis.

children.title: Impedance-based circuit laws
children.description: Impedance extends Ohm's and Kirchhoff's laws to AC circuits.

children.title: AC circuit solution methods
children.description: The same nodal, mesh, and equivalent-circuit tools work in the phasor domain.

topics.title: Phasors and Impedance
topics.description: Phasors and impedance are the bridge between time-domain sinusoidal signals and algebraic circuit calculations.

children.title: Phasor transformation
children.description: Phasor transformation turns sinusoidal time functions into complex constants for easier analysis.

children.title: Impedance and admittance
children.description: Impedance and admittance summarize how circuit elements oppose or admit sinusoidal current.

children.title: Phase relationships
children.description: Phase tells students whether voltage and current are aligned, leading, or lagging.

children.title: Frequency-dependent behavior
children.description: Impedance changes with frequency, which is the core idea behind filters and resonance.

topics.title: Power in DC and AC Circuits
topics.description: Power analysis connects circuit behavior to energy use, heating, source sizing, efficiency, and real-world electrical safety.

children.title: DC power
children.description: DC power calculations show where energy is delivered and dissipated in resistive circuits.

children.title: AC average power
children.description: Average power captures real energy transfer in sinusoidal steady state.

children.title: Reactive and apparent power
children.description: Reactive and apparent power explain energy exchange in inductive and capacitive systems.

children.title: Practical power considerations
children.description: Practical circuits must account for ratings, heat, and safe operating limits.

topics.title: Frequency Response and Filters
topics.description: Frequency response explains how circuits treat different signal frequencies, while filters turn that behavior into useful design patterns.

children.title: Transfer functions
children.description: A transfer function describes output-input behavior as a function of frequency or complex variable.

children.title: Bode plots
children.description: Bode plots make magnitude and phase behavior visible over wide frequency ranges.

children.title: Passive filters
children.description: Passive filters use R, L, and C elements to select or reject frequency bands.

children.title: Active filters
children.description: Active filters use op-amps to add gain, buffering, and sharper frequency shaping.

topics.title: Measurement, Simulation, and Practical Debugging
topics.description: A circuits course should not stop at equations. Students need to measure real circuits, simulate ideas, and debug when physical behavior disagrees with the schematic.

children.title: Simulation tools
children.description: Simulation helps students test circuit behavior quickly and visualize voltage, current, and transient response.

children.title: Bench instruments
children.description: Measurement skills connect theory to hardware and teach what circuit quantities actually look like.

children.title: Prototyping practice
children.description: Prototyping exposes nonideal details that paper analysis often hides.

children.title: Debugging workflow
children.description: Debugging teaches students to isolate faults systematically instead of changing parts at random.
